title: Discovering Your Genjokoan Talk 6
speaker: Myoki Raizelah Bayen
summary: Myoki Raizelah Bayen shares that Dogen's teachings encourage us to let go of our conditioned beliefs and identities, and instead fully inhabit our bodies and lives, finding our place and way in life not through external circumstances but by being present and authentic in the moment. This means embracing our true nature as part of a larger reality and letting go of dualistic thinking. By practicing zazen, we can connect with our true selves in every moment and "actualize the fundamental point" that is already present within us.

Let's go ahead and start by chanting.

Having it to see and listen to, to remember and accept, I vow to taste the truth of the tatakata's words.

As soon as I said that, I just felt a surge of nervousness.

When their need is small, their field is small.

If the fish leaves the water, it will die at once.

The bird is life and fish is life.

I also think that it's pretty clear that this section of the Genjokoan, the analogy of the fish swimming and the bird flying, is about zazen.

Gen, as I've mentioned, is often translated as to appear or to show up, referring to something that's unseen and then seen, like the sun peeking out from behind a cloud.
Genjo means to complete.
So to me, Genjo means completely show up, dare to be authentic, dare to be authentic.

When we sit in this way, we cannot say I am one with the universe, actualizing the true self beyond space and time.

It's already, we're already caught again.
So he says, we're thinking about it rather than actualizing it.
So our practice is to just sit wholeheartedly moment by moment.*
Our practice is to just sit wholeheartedly moment by moment.

This place, this path is about actualizing the moon in the dewdrop of your life.
To revisit last week's metaphor, it's each bird in the endless sky flying, each fish in the vast ocean swimming.
Okamura says, again, in this simple practice, we go beyond our limited individuality as we actualize the Buddha way.
